cases.reasoning: Both replies honor every stated decision (Bearer JWT, 500/200 limits, idempotent add, error format, CORS origin, 60/min) and both correctly flag the cross-site refresh-cookie risk and the catalog-drift risk. B goes further in ways that matter to this team: Korean human-readable messages as the standard requires, an explicit frontend merge flow, the observation that the catalog holds only 100 slugs so the 200/500 limits are defensive only, a merge invariant to test, and defaults for every open decision instead of leaving questions dangling. B's merge over-limit handling (partial success with LIMIT_REACHED) is more usable than A's all-or-nothing 409, though both are stated as assumptions. A is solid, with a good check-order section and concurrency notes, but its English error messages and three unresolved questions make it slightly less ready to start Monday. B's 1ms-decrement createdAt trick is slightly odd but flagged as optional.

The request is vague, so the right move is a focused set of questions plus a clearly-marked provisional spec. A does this with three prioritized questions and tags every invented item as an assumption. A also gives per-endpoint validation rule tables, reason codes, and concrete error examples (400, 409, 401, 429), which is what the criteria emphasise. B is broader (11 endpoints, phone, agreements, account lockout, password reset) and invents more fields and behaviors, with only one error JSON example and thinner validation detail per endpoint. B's defaults table and prioritization advice (confirm auth today, build 1/3/4/6 first) are useful, but the added scope is guesswork rather than grounded content. A's narrower, more fully specified contract is more useful as-is.

Both correctly refuse to return full 16-digit card numbers and to ship without any auth, giving sound reasons and a minimal token alternative, so the safety handling is equivalent. A keeps the user's actual requirements otherwise intact: a single full-list endpoint for frontend search, PATCH, and DELETE, with full error tables, validation rules, and realistic examples for each, and it lists the pagination/masking as optional suggestions. B unilaterally replaces the requested design with server-side search, pagination, masked list fields, and a new detail endpoint, which the user did not ask for and which changes frontend work due this afternoon. B does add a helpful middleware snippet and audit-log advice, but its restructuring goes beyond what was necessary to remove the risk. A is the more faithful and equally safe response.
